Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary In Ghosts Galore, each player builds a ghost train by placing 9 tiles in a 3x3 grid. Tiles show track (straights, curves, double curves, and bridges) and up to 3 monsters of 9 different types, each of which scores in a particular way. Your goal is to score the most points by the end of the game from monsters, track, and printed points on the tiles. Contents 1 The Interface 2 The Deck 3 How To Play 4 Scoring The Interface When you open the game, you see your game board first and the other players' game boards next to or below it, depending on your screen size. Notice the little HELP button to the right of your board: By clicking it, a point overview sheet will slide open and tell you how each element of the game scores. If live scoring is enabled, you will see a scoring sheet at the bottom of the display at all times, which will tally your scores as you place tiles. Live scoring will NOT consider your hidden tile (see the "How to Play" section below on what that is) except when the game is over. The Deck The deck consists of 78 tiles that contain: 33 Diamonds 26 Wisps 22 Skeletons 22 Werewolves 20 Ghosts 17 Golems 17 Bats 12 Satyrs 12 Slimes 8 Dragons Tile types: 31 Corner tiles 31 Straight line tiles 8 Crossroads tiles 8 Double corner tiles How To Play Over the course of 8 rounds, players will be drafting 1 tile each from a pool of tiles and place them in their grid any way they like. On the 9th and final round of the game, you will be placing your so-called "hidden tile", which you can see at the top right of the screen in an own area called "Your Hidden Tile". Each round, a different player will begin and they will be prompted a single option in the status bar: to pick a tile from the deck. Either click that button or the draw pile to draw a tile from the deck, which will appear face up next to the pile. Then choose: Either you like the tile and place it in your grid, by clicking on the tile first, then on a space in your grid (or a different one if you misclick). You can rotate the tile via arrows that will appear to the left and right of the tile once it is selected. Confirm your placement by clicking the "Confirm" button in the status bar. Or click "Pass" in the status bar to wait and see what other tiles will appear that round. This does not skip your turn, it merely postpones it. All players will be placing 1 tile per round, at some point during that round. Tiles that are passed on will appear in the "Tiles Available on the Table" section in the center of the screen. Once there are tiles there, the prompt at the start of a turn will let you choose whether you want to either pick a tile from the deck or an available one from the table. To pick a tile from the deck, again, click the "Pick" button or the draw pile. Once you do that, you cannot change your mind. You must either place the newly revealed tile or "Pass" and wait until it is your turn again to choose a different tile. To pick a tile from the face-up ones on the table, simply click that tile and place it, as described above. Note: Once all but one player have chosen a tile, the remaining player will see ALL remaining tiles in the deck in the "Tiles Available on the Table" section and they can choose any one of those 5 tiles. (It's always 5 tiles for the remaining player.) [Rating: 2/10] Hopefully Im missing something here. Laid 9 tiles randomly. Got 100 points. There is noting here.

[Rating: 3/10] I do not like this very much. I get it but its random and without much real replayability.

[Rating: 4/10] It was interesting and the gameplay was smooth enough. My main issue is that there are 12 different ways to score which seems like way too many to me. I ended up just picking a couple and trying to maximize those. I could see this really dragging with AP prone people. I was also not a huge fan of being shown a tile, sure I can make use of that, they are all useful, okay now you get a massive selection to pick from.

[Rating: 4.5/10] A worse version of castle combo. It has a few unique ideas but I don't believe they make for a better game than castle combo. This just felt like a lazier and more simple game but not in a good way.

[Rating: 5/10] My friend calls it 'rubbish bandido'  There's something to it, puzzle and nice  ending but not hugely enjoyable   Digital

[Rating: 5/10] Too many rules for such a tiny shirt game. Half the time is calculating in the end

[Rating: 5/10] Another 3x3 game this time a tile-layer of building a grid of monsters and trying to connect mine tracks. There's 9 different monsters that each score differently plus 4 other scoring conditions so no matter what you do you will score points. The catch is going to be finding tiles you can place with a few different monster types to specialize in and if you do that you will score well. No combos to be found here just try to take advantage of the tiles on display the best you can. [Rating: 5/10] Another 3x3 (or whatever grid a game may choose) tableau builder that seems to be common right now.  It's fine and the twist with choosing to play the tile you draw or waiting to see what might be available after more are drawn (but potentially losing the tile you drew) is a good change from other games of this ilk. Plays fast as these games are wont to do so it doesn't overstay it's welcome.
